extracted.intended_audience: students in Don Knuth's writing/course (computer science/math students) and technical authors preparing term papers, articles, or books
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and preparing technical papers/term papers (especially in computer science/mathematics), covering quotation practice, exposition strategy, editing interactions, and typesetting considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation: acceptable motives and the chief anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer quotes words used before because they give his meaning better than he can, because they are beautiful or witty, or because he expects them to touch a chord in readers, or because he wishes to show that he is learned and well-read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation done merely to display learning is 'invariably ill-advised'; the discerning reader detects it and is contemptuous, the undiscerning perhaps impressed but repelled. Use quotations for clarity, beauty, resonance, not pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding apt quotations (resources and methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation dictionaries (Bartlett's Familiar Quotations), the OED (which prints memorable quotations in word entries), concordances (e.g., Shakespeare/Chaucer), and modern electronic/text searches to locate quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with Bartlett under relevant index headings; when Bartlett fails, try the OED or concordances; computer searches make it easy to search texts (example: finding 'comma' in Camus). Examples: Don used Bartlett for 'technique'; used online texts to find occurrences of words across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting apposite quotations (including out-of-context use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select quotations that are apposite to the passage you are introducing or concluding, even if taken out of context, provided they illuminate or frame the subject appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don often used quotations taken out of context (economist Leontief for 'output', Galsworthy on 'Expressionists'); in a pinch quote yourself or solicit a brief comment from someone prominent. Aim for quotations that enhance tone or introduce a theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotations sparingly and purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations should be used when they provide a meaning or effect the writer cannot as well provide themselves; avoid overusing quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate serendipity (wide reading) to find good quotations, but don't employ quotation primarily to signal erudition. Prefer quotes that genuinely contribute to the reader's understanding or enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: include and use indexes conscientiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Indices are important navigational aids for readers; if something isn't in the index, readers may still search the whole work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sears & Roebuck 1899 advice: 'If you don't find it in the index, look very carefully through the entire catalogue.' (Humorous) Recognize the value of good indexing; some advocated legislation to compel indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph layout and indentation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of paragraph indentation and line lengths so pages look balanced; ensure last line of a paragraph is at least as long as the indentation on the following one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don found designers had large paragraph indentations, requiring him to add/subtract words so the last line length matched the following indentation; poor matching makes the page look strange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a genre in mind and do a good job in that genre
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a term paper or piece of exposition, choose and respect an appropriate genre and write well within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don recommended trying to have a genre in mind (e.g., expository essay, dialog, tutorial) and to do the genre well; examples included Woody Allen spoof and dialogues like Lamport's or Knuth's Surreal Numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a general audience at least once; remove jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt writing for non-specialist readers to practice clear exposition; technical pieces should avoid unnecessary jargon to be more accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don praised editors' work in removing jargon to make material accessible to general readers (Scientific American example). George Forsythe suggested every scientist try writing for general readers at least once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage cooperatively with editors and insist on proof review
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect editing when submitting to general-audience outlets; engage constructively with editors, request proofs, and correct typographical/semantic errors introduced by editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's Scientific American saga: editors rewrote many sentences, introduced and removed commas, changed 'which' to 'that', etc. He negotiated changes, requested galley proofs (unusual), and used the proof stage to correct math/typographic errors. Viewing proofs is important especially for technical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect editorial changes but evaluate them critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Some editorial changes improve clarity; others may introduce errors or alter technical meaning; authors should review edits critically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don found some SA edits gratuitous or introducing errors; after re-editing and proof negotiation he acknowledged some edits were appropriate while others were not. Maintain dialogue with editors and be willing to accept beneficial changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting of mathematical notation and typographic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical typesetting requires special care: brackets vs parentheses have specific meanings, numeric formatting differs between text and formulas, and certain typographic conventions (e.g., 'lg' vs 'log') must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: floor brackets restored where square brackets appeared; IEEE/ACM changes (writing 'zero'/'one' vs '0'/'1'); 'lg' changed to 'log' causing ambiguity; number grouping conventions differ (1,000,000 vs 10^6 vs 1 234 567 vs spaces). Authors should check proofs and insist on preserving precise notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display of equations and the expectations of different outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Some general-audience outlets (e.g., Scientific American) avoid displaying equations; authors should be aware of an outlet's policy on equations and adapt accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SA 'never display equations'; some readers refuse to read outlets that hide equations. Know the audience and publication norms when preparing manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number formatting policy awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that publishers may apply different conventions for formatting numbers (commas, spaces, grouping), and these may be applied differently in running text vs formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don objected to inserting commas in formulas (1,000,000) whereas publisher suggested 10^6; IEEE uses spaces (1 234 567) in numerics. Decide what's appropriate for formulas vs text and check proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and naming: choose names carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and terminology matter; choose terms that convey meaning and consider community usage to avoid later regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Automata Theory' sanctioned though awkward; regrets about names used in TAoCP (Daemon vs Oracle); community polls may rename concepts (Polynomially-complete → NP-complete). If possible, pick names thoughtfully but be pragmatic about community adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository techniques: motivate with puzzles and examples; build reader intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use puzzles, motivating examples, and concrete problems to build the right mental structures in the reader and prepare them for formal algorithms/proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don used a puzzle to motivate a difficult theorem and algorithm, saying this primes the reader's mind. Use examples to show nontriviality and to create intuition before presenting formal material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider unconventional formats (dialog, Q&A) when suitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialog and question-and-answer formats can be effective exposition devices to present ideas clearly and engagingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport's Q&A style and Knuth's Surreal Numbers dialog are cited as successful uses of such formats; dialogs can make material more accessible and lively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage complexity: handle many cases but seek unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer science often requires handling many cases; while detailed casework is a strength, authors should also look for unifying perspectives where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don noted that 'the ability to handle lots of cases is Computer Science's strength and weakness' and encouraged seeking unity when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for language/translation issues in international publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators face challenges with technical terms (e.g., 'hashing'); authors should be prepared to advise or accept varied translations and not assume direct equivalents exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'hashing' becomes long in Chinese; French translators consult language academies for equivalents. When writing for international audiences, consider translation implications and possibly supply clarifying notes.
